clinicalPearls: Results from ischaemic necrosis of the pituitary following severe postpartum haemorrhage and hypotension
Failure to lactate after delivery is often the earliest clue, reflecting prolactin deficiency
Failure to resume menstruation and loss of pubic and axillary hair point to gonadotrophin and adrenal androgen loss
The clinical picture can be insidious, sometimes emerging years after the index pregnancy, and is frequently missed
The enlarged, vascular pregnant pituitary is especially vulnerable to hypoperfusion, explaining the peripartum timing
Corticotroph deficiency may present acutely as an adrenal crisis, particularly under physiological stress
Diabetes insipidus is uncommon because the posterior pituitary is usually relatively spared
Imaging may later reveal an empty or partially empty sella from pituitary atrophy
reference.pathophysiology: Sheehan syndrome arises when major obstetric haemorrhage and circulatory collapse cause ischaemic infarction of the anterior pituitary. During pregnancy the gland hypertrophies, largely due to lactotroph expansion, increasing its metabolic demand while its low-pressure portal blood supply leaves it prone to infarction if perfusion falls. The resulting loss of anterior pituitary tissue produces variable, often panhypopituitary, hormone deficiencies affecting prolactin, gonadotrophins, growth hormone, thyroid-stimulating hormone and corticotrophin. The posterior lobe is usually preserved, so diabetes insipidus is comparatively rare, and the infarcted gland gradually atrophies, sometimes leaving an empty sella.
additionalDifferentials: Empty sella syndrome from other causes
Primary autoimmune endocrine failure such as thyroid or adrenal disease
Depression or other non-endocrine causes of postpartum fatigue
additionalInvestigations: Anterior pituitary hormone profile including cortisol, thyroid and gonadal axes
Dynamic pituitary testing where basal results are equivocal
Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary, which may show an empty sella
Serum electrolytes to detect hyponatraemia from cortisol or thyroid deficiency
Documentation of the obstetric history and any peripartum haemorrhage
redFlags: Adrenal crisis with hypotension and hyponatraemia
Profound fatigue and collapse under physiological stress
Delayed diagnosis leading to chronic untreated hypopituitarism
reference.prognosis: With appropriate and lifelong hormone replacement, patients generally do well, but unrecognised disease carries a real risk of life-threatening adrenal crisis; deficits are permanent because infarcted pituitary tissue does not recover.
pitfalls: Attributing failed lactation and fatigue to normal postpartum recovery and missing the diagnosis
Starting thyroid hormone before glucocorticoid replacement and precipitating adrenal crisis
Failing to consider the diagnosis years after the causative delivery
Overlooking hyponatraemia as a manifestation of cortisol or thyroid deficiency
Assuming posterior pituitary involvement and over-investigating for diabetes insipidus
management: Lifelong anterior pituitary hormone replacement, replacing glucocorticoid first to avoid precipitating adrenal crisis
Levothyroxine for secondary hypothyroidism once adequate glucocorticoid cover is established
Oestrogen with progestogen replacement for gonadotrophin deficiency until the usual age of menopause, and growth hormone replacement in selected adults
Stress-dose glucocorticoid cover during illness, surgery, or physiological stress, with a steroid emergency card and patient education
Urgent parenteral hydrocortisone and fluid resuscitation for adrenal crisis
Monitor clinical and biochemical adequacy of replacement, including electrolytes for hyponatraemia
